1|## Problem
2|
3|Baton2 session and provider logs consume multiple gigabytes during normal coordination work. On 2026-10-06 the development host had approximately 0.8 GiB free, and worker attempts reported ENOSPC. Storage exhaustion interrupted task recovery and provider execution.
4|
5|Measured examples from the canonical Baton2 workspace:
6|
7|- `semantic-impl-context-core.jsonl`: 819,516,444 bytes.
8|- `semantic-impl-codec.jsonl`: approximately 739 MB allocated.
9|- A recovery DeepSeek provider log: approximately 811 MB allocated.
10|- The cleanup inventory found approximately 20.9 GiB of inactive JSONL and log candidates across Baton workspaces and agent history directories. This aggregate includes external harness histories; ownership and amplification must be measured separately.
11|
12|APFS compression preserves existing evidence and provides immediate relief. Baton2 needs practical defaults that control the amount of data generated and retained.
13|
14|## Requested work
15|
16|Create a new conductor-led ensemble with implementation and independent validation Players. Inspect every Baton2-owned log producer, harness adapter, subprocess capture, replay path, and native session report extractor. Measure event counts, repeated snapshots, duplicated tool payloads, cumulative streaming output, token chunks, and retained artifacts to identify the actual sources of amplification.
17|
18|Implement a practical logging system with:
19|
20|- Concise default operational events that retain session, actor, turn, message, tool, error, exit, delivery, and validation identifiers needed for debugging and recovery.
21|- Explicit verbosity settings with documented behavior for normal operation and targeted debugging. Expensive full provider traces must have a clear activation and retention policy.
22|- References to retained payload artifacts when repeated large data would otherwise be copied into logs. Preserve necessary evidence and access paths.
23|- Rotation, compression, retention, and cleanup rules for logs owned by Baton2, with configurable storage budgets and visible diagnostics. Determine defaults from measurements and operational requirements.
24|- Clear ownership boundaries for external harness histories, session databases, pending messages, dirty worktrees, and validation evidence.
25|- Correct handling of write failures and disk exhaustion so completion and delivery reports remain accurate.
26|- A safe way to inspect storage use and preview cleanup, followed by explicit cleanup of eligible artifacts.
27|
28|Do not delete unresolved messages, source changes, credentials, active traces, or the only retained delivery/validation evidence. Retention must account for incomplete tasks and pending inputs. Coordinate with #685, #666, #669, #664, and #670 so smaller logs preserve report extraction, error diagnosis, and continuation behavior.
29|
30|## Acceptance evidence
31|
32|1. A reproducible representative coordination workload with before/after bytes per event and turn, peak file size, total retained bytes, and useful diagnostic coverage.
33|2. Demonstrated reduction of log generation and retained storage, with the measured reduction and chosen defaults justified in the issue.
34|3. Tests for repeated streaming output, large tool payloads, rotation, restart/replay, incomplete turns, failed writes, retention eligibility, and concurrent readers/writers.
35|4. Independent validation that pending-message recovery, provider error reporting, native report extraction, and delivery/validation evidence remain usable.
36|5. Scoped commits, push to the assigned remote branch, appropriate CI and runtime validation, and an accurate delivery report identifying any remaining gates.

Read text file `AGENTS.md`.
1|# Rules for this project
2|
3|These rules apply to every agent and harness working on baton, not only Claude. The first section
4|applies to code and design. The rest apply to prose.
5|
6|## Validation execution
7|
8|The operator's laptop hosts orchestration, source edits and evidence review.
9|Compilation, compiler checks, build and test gates, and CI/CD execute on remote
10|validation runners. Homelab runners provide Linux capacity; platform-specific
11|acceptance uses a remote runner for that platform. Preserve exact source and
12|toolchain identity, full output and completed process evidence for each run.
13|
14|A background validation process remains owned until its recorded completion.
15|Continue through the existing execution handle when a tool returns a running
16|job. Repeated requests for that active execution must retain its ownership and
17|result. The observed duplicate fixture build and crash evidence are recorded
18|in `docs/bend2/host-crash-2026-10-05.md`.
19|
20|# Banned runtime patterns
21|
22|## No pausing, idling or truncating agents
23|
24|Baton never deliberately pauses, idles or truncates an agent's work. When an agent's turn ends,
25|Baton wakes the agent's orchestrator (its parent seat, or the root) with the turn's report, and the
26|orchestrator decides whether to nudge the agent on. The agent stops when it declares itself done or
27|its orchestrator stops it. No runtime rule may leave live work waiting on a party that Baton does not
28|wake. An existing instance is a `priority:high` bug to remove (#572). The first known instance is
29|the turn-end park recorded under the actor `policy`, which waits for a claim or nudge and wakes no
30|one.
31|
32|## No bookkeeping ledgers in place of function
33|
34|Do not model code changes or test outcomes as entries in a hand-maintained ledger. That means no
35|checked-in list of expected test failures, no "converged" declarations, no census file, and no test
36|that pins counts or line numbers of other code. A landing gate answers one question: does this change
37|break something that works on the target? It runs the selected tests on the target and on the
38|change, and blocks only on a test that passes on the target and fails with the change. Known breakage
39|lives in the issue tracker. The existing expected-red manifest is being removed (#580); do not add to it.
40|
41|# Writing rules
42|
43|These rules apply to any prose written for or checked into this repository: README, CONTRIBUTING,
44|`docs/*.md`, issue and PR bodies, commit messages, code comments, and anything else meant to be
45|read by a person.
46|
47|## Plain technical English only
48|
49|Write in plain, simplified, standard technical English. No aphorism, no metaphor, no poetic
50|description, no narrative flourish. A section heading names what the section covers; it is not a
51|place for cleverness (write "Design documents", not "the swarm era"; cut lines like "the name: a
52|conductor's baton directs an orchestra").
53|
54|## State facts directly, never by contrast to an absent alternative
55|
56|Never describe a mechanism by contrasting it with something the project does not do or does not
57|have ("wakes instead of polling", "typed refusals instead of free-text errors", "verification is
58|re-run, not trusted"). This pattern says what the thing is not rather than what it is, and it reads
59|as marketing rhetoric, not a technical description. State directly what the thing does.
60|
61|- Wrong: "Wakes instead of polling."
62|- Right: "`baton swarm watch --follow` prints one JSON frame per coordination row as it is written."
63|
64|If an entire section is organized around this contrast (a "why choose this" framing built on a list
65|of things the project avoids), restructure or cut it — its real content usually already lives
66|elsewhere once each fact is stated positively.
67|
68|## No gratuitous or generic commentary
69|
70|Cut any aside that states something true of any tool in the category, not specific to this
71|project. ("directs workers, on your own repository" — of course a CLI run in a repository operates
72|on that repository; this told the reader nothing about baton.) Every sentence should carry
73|information a reader could not already assume.
74|
75|## No operational journaling in product-facing documentation
76|
77|A README, or any document meant to describe the product to someone encountering it, describes what
78|the software is and does. It does not narrate the project's own development process, internal
79|workflow, or history as a feature of the product ("every change since <date> has gone through our
80|own X process" does not belong in a README). Facts about how the project itself is developed
81|belong in CONTRIBUTING.md or a docs/ ledger such as docs/PROGRESS.md, written for the audience that
82|is actually doing that work, not folded into the pitch for the software.
83|
84|## Audience-appropriate density
85|
86|`docs/*.md` design documents are written for contributors already working in this codebase and may
87|cite issue numbers (`#441`) and internal mechanism names densely; that is the correct register for
88|that audience. README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md's introduction, and anything else meant to introduce the
89|project to someone new must not assume the reader has the issue tracker open, and should explain a
90|mechanism rather than pointing at a bare issue number with no context.
91|
92|See the `writing-style` skill for the same rules with worked before/after examples.
